description: A study the King commissioned himself finds the House of Orange supported colonialism for centuries and earned the equivalent of nearly 576 million euros from it. The prime minister has ruled out new reparations. Also today: inflation rises on fuel prices, a court backs stricter family reunification rules, banks tighten mortgages for over-fifties, a planned tax on vapes, the Golden Calf winners, and seventy-five years of Dutch TV.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The Dutch royal family backed colonialism for centuries and earned the equivalent of more than half a billion euros from it. That's the finding of a huge study the King asked for himself.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: He calls it heartbreaking. The prime minister says there'll be no new reparations.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Also today: inflation ticks up, a court ruling on family reunification, and Dutch TV turns seventy-five. It's Saturday, the third of October. I'm Maya.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And I'm Sam. This is Dutch Daily Briefing.

segments.title: The House of Orange and its colonial past

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: We start in Leiden, where the King was handed a study of his own family's colonial past on Friday.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Wait, he commissioned that himself?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: He asked for it and he paid for it. About sixty researchers worked on it, led by historian Gert Oostindie. And the verdict is blunt. Oostindie says every stadtholder, king and queen, at least up to Queen Wilhelmina, believed colonialism was legitimate. And they gave it active and unscrupulous support for centuries. That includes slavery, for as long as it existed.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Stadtholders being the Orange leaders before the country had a king. So how much money are we talking?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The equivalent of nearly five hundred and seventy-six million euros in today's money. Almost all of it came from the Dutch East India Company and the former Dutch East Indies, now Indonesia.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Not from the Atlantic slave trade?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Almost nothing came from that, but only because the West India Company lost them money. Not because they objected. And the researchers say little of the colonial money is left today.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Did the royals actually set colonial policy?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Rarely. The exception is King William the First, who in 1828 looked for ways around laws against the slave trade. And the study calls Queen Wilhelmina the most imperialist. In 1947 she wrote that she had no objection to so-called police actions against Indonesian independence.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The King called the findings heartbreaking and confronting. He said, I cannot change the past, but I can make a positive contribution to the present and the future. What he didn't mention was money.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And Prime Minister Rob Jetten ruled out new reparations. He pointed to the two hundred million euros set aside in 2023 for education and remembrance, and to plans to return colonial-era art.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That didn't satisfy everyone. NiNsee, the national slavery heritage institute, welcomed the report but wants talks on repair. And activist Mitchell Esajas of The Black Archives handed back his royal honour. He said words about reconciliation aren't enough.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So the history's on the record now. What to do about it is another argument.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Now, your wallet, and what it costs to fill up the tank.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Dutch inflation rose to three point four percent in September, up a touch from August. That's a first estimate from CBS, the national statistics bureau.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And let me guess, fuel's to blame?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Mostly. Motor fuel and heating energy cost almost fourteen percent more than a year ago. Advisory pump prices are above two euros seventy a litre, though what people actually pay is lower on average.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Any good news?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Groceries. They got cheaper for the second month in a row. But CBS chief economist Peter Hein van Mulligen warns that high energy prices usually reach shop prices after about six months. He doesn't expect a spike like 2022, though.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That's the year inflation here hit double digits.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Eurozone inflation is even higher, at three point eight percent. Before the war in Iran, it was just under two.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And there's an oil story on top of all this.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: There is. The G7 agreed to release up to a hundred million barrels of diesel and crude from emergency reserves over four months, with a lot of the diesel in the first twenty days. That came after pressure from President Trump, who'd threatened to ban US diesel exports. Europe now gets much of its diesel from the US.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Is the Netherlands chipping in? It's not in the G7.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It's already drawing on its own reserves under an earlier deal from March, and it released another batch on Thursday. It hasn't said whether it'll add more. And there's no new cut in fuel tax, just a slower phase-out of the existing discount next year.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So don't expect much relief at the pump. The final inflation figures are out on the thirteenth of October.

segments.title: Court backs stricter family reunification rules

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Next, a court ruling that matters for refugees hoping to bring their families here.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: This is about the stricter family reunification rules, right?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yes. Since the twelfth of June, the Netherlands has had a two-status system, introduced alongside the EU's new Asylum and Migration Pact. It treats recognised refugees more generously than people with subsidiary protection.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Subsidiary protection meaning what, exactly?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: You're not recognised as a refugee, but it isn't safe for you to go home. Under the new rules, those people have to wait two years before applying to bring family over. And they need housing that's suitable for the whole family.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So the question is what happens to people who applied before June.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Exactly. Two Syrians with subsidiary protection applied under the old rules, but the IND, the immigration service, rejected them under the new ones. The law has no transitional arrangement. On Friday, the district court in The Hague said that's allowed.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Even though they applied under the old system?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The court acknowledged the effects can be serious, especially for them. But it found the rules don't break higher law or general legal principles. It's the court's first ruling on the new system.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: How many people does this affect?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: When the rules took effect, more than nineteen thousand people were waiting for a decision on family reunification. It's not clear how many of them have subsidiary protection.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And it's not over yet. The Syrians' lawyer is appealing, and the refugee charity VluchtelingenWerk says the Council of State, the top administrative court, will have the final word. No date's been set for that ruling.

segments.title: Banks cut mortgages for older buyers

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Now, mortgages, and some bad news if you're in your fifties.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Go on, ruin my Saturday.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Rabobank and ABN Amro, two of the biggest Dutch banks, are cutting how much older buyers can borrow. From next March, Rabobank and its subsidiary Obvion will start counting expected pension income fifteen years before retirement, instead of ten.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And pension income is usually lower than a salary, so the maximum mortgage drops.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Right. With the state pension age at sixty-seven, that hits applicants from fifty-two. Rabobank will also factor in life expectancy. At eighty-five and over, you'll be able to borrow at most seventy percent of your home's value.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And ABN Amro?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Similar changes from the ninth of December, according to the trade site InFinance. It keeps the ten-year threshold but will check whether your income after retirement is enough. And at eighty-five, it caps borrowing at half the home's value.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Why is this happening now?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Because of new guidance from DNB, the Dutch central bank. It wants banks to make sure pension income can carry the loan. And it treats any part of a loan that outlasts your life expectancy like interest-only debt, repaid mainly by selling the house.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Who gets hit hardest?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Self-employed people with little pension savings. The mortgage data firm IEX worked out that someone relying only on the state pension might qualify for a mortgage of about a hundred thousand euros.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: At Rabobank, the rules cover new customers and anyone refinancing, but existing loans left unchanged aren't affected. ING hasn't announced anything yet, but others in the sector expect more lenders to follow.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Staying with things that are about to cost more: vapes.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Let me guess. A new tax?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: From January 2029, the government plans an excise tax on vapes and refills, on top of the twenty-one percent VAT. The rate isn't set yet, but the aim is to make vapes about as expensive as tobacco. Eelco Eerenberg, the junior finance minister from D66, says it's shocking how many young people are vaping.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And the numbers back him up. In the latest schools survey, more than one in five pupils aged twelve to sixteen had tried a vape. About one in eight had vaped in the past month.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Eerenberg says higher prices will make people think twice about spending money on, his words, unhealthy junk. And that the health of our children cannot wait for Brussels.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Why would it be waiting for Brussels?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Because he admits vapes are easy to buy online or across the border, so the government would really prefer an EU-wide tax. But EU tax rules need all twenty-seven member states on board. In June, EU finance ministers dropped the plan from their agenda because they couldn't agree.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And if Brussels does act after all?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: If an EU tax arrives before 2029, the Dutch plan gets withdrawn. The bill should reach the Tweede Kamer, the House of Representatives, early next year.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Worth remembering that vapes in any flavour other than tobacco have been banned here since 2024, though in practice that ban's often ignored. And from 2027 or 2028, vapes should only be sold in specialist shops.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Here in Amsterdam, the city has backed down on a plan for Utrechtsestraat.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That's the busy shopping street running from Rembrandtplein to Frederiksplein. Trams, bikes, delivery vans and pedestrians, all squeezed together.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's the one. Earlier this year, the city proposed making it one-way. It said the street was unsafe and that more than forty-two hundred vehicles a day used it. Southbound traffic would have kept the street, and northbound traffic would have been sent through side streets.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And now that's off. What happened?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Residents pushed back, hard. Several neighbourhood groups feared it would just push traffic onto nearby streets. They challenged the city's traffic figures and did their own counts.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Residents doing their own traffic counts. Very Amsterdam.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: A neighbourhood survey got more than five hundred responses. Most people said the street felt safe, and close to nine in ten were against one-way traffic. The small-business group MKB Metropool Amsterdam was against it too.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So what does the city do instead?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Smaller fixes. An extra zebra crossing, changes at the Frederiksplein junction, checks on loading and unloading, speed checks and speed bumps.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Is that final?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Not yet. It's still a proposal from the Centrum district's executive. The district committee discusses it on Monday, before the final decision.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So if you cycle down Utrechtsestraat, expect a few more bumps, not a whole new route.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Sam, the Golden Calves have been handed out, the country's top film and TV prizes.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Still my favourite trophy name. Very Old Testament.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The big winner was Truly Naked, the first feature by Muriel d'Ansembourg. It won six of its seven nominations, including best film.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And here's the thing for our listeners: it's in English. It follows Alec, an introverted British boy growing up in his dad's low-budget porn business.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So, not a cosy family movie night. It's streaming now on Pathé Thuis and Picl. The other big winner was Basta, the Videoland series about Marco van Basten.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: For the non-football fans, he's one of the greatest Dutch players ever. He scored that famous volley in the 1988 Euros final, and that's still the national team's only major title. The series won three awards, including best actor for Chris Peters.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Meanwhile the favourite, Joe Speedboot, had nine nominations and won just one. And Halina Reijn, who directed Nicole Kidman in Babygirl, got a career award. She called herself a farmer's girl in Hollywood.

segments.title: Hans Anders pulls Meta camera glasses

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Maya, camera glasses. A big Dutch optician has just pulled them off its shelves.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's Hans Anders, the budget chain on pretty much every Dutch high street. It's stopped selling Meta's AI glasses, made with Ray-Ban, both in its shops and online.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: They look like normal glasses, but they take photos and video hands-free. A tiny light flickers while they're recording. And critics here have a great nickname for them: gluurbril. Peeping glasses.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Ouch. Hans Anders pointed to the public and political debate. It says it had only sold limited numbers anyway, at four hundred and nineteen euros and up.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And the debate's heating up. Two groups, including the abuse victims' support group Offlimits, have given Meta two weeks to stop selling them or face court. And the Tweede Kamer passed a motion asking the cabinet to further restrict wearing them, with exceptions for medical use.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The cabinet's reluctant, though. It wants to wait for an EU assessment that's expected this autumn.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And if you really want a pair, Pearle, Specsavers and MediaMarkt are still selling them. Maybe just warn your friends before you hit record.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Finally, Dutch television turned seventy-five this week.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Seventy-five! The Netherlands was a bit late to the party, wasn't it?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Very late. The BBC had been broadcasting since 1936. The Dutch beat Denmark by just one day.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: A photo finish.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The first broadcast was a ninety-minute live show from a studio in Bussum, with a live performance of a play called The Magic Mirror. Thousands watched through radio shop windows or in cafés.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Because hardly anyone had a set. There were about five hundred in the whole country, and each one cost a third of an average yearly income.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And the government wasn't keen. Prime Minister Willem Drees wanted money spent on housing, not luxuries, and he feared TV would distract workers and corrupt young people. The head of the broadcasters even warned on air about television's harmful influence.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Getting the warning in early. I respect that.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The government only gave in when Philips threatened to set up television itself. And even then, it was approved as a two-year experiment.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Some experiment. Media historian Huub Wijfjes says TV is still the dominant medium.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: If you'd rather get off the sofa tonight, here's what's on in Amsterdam today. The big one: the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra plays the Ziggo Dome in Zuidoost at eight.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That's classical highlights in an arena, conducted by Iván Fischer, and it ends with Beethoven's Ninth. The whole audience is invited to sing along to the Ode to Joy.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: There's even an optional sing-along rehearsal from seven, and ticket holders get practice material in advance. Tickets are through Mojo.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Count me in, humming at the back. Something calmer? Camera Japan, the biggest Japanese film festival in the Benelux, is on at LAB111 in Oud-West from half past twelve until ten. Anime, arthouse, classics, plus food and music. It runs until Sunday, but check the website, because times may change.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And for a morning wander, there's a free antiques, curiosities and vintage market at the Oosterkerk in the eastern city centre, from nine to five. One day only.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That's it for today. I'm Sam.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And I'm Maya. Thanks for listening to Dutch Daily Briefing. Enjoy your Saturday, and talk soon.
